slides.title: Physical To Virtual
slides.body:
Virtualization Landscape
Virtualization uses software to create virtual versions of computing resources, allowing physical hardware to be shared efficiently while keeping workloads isolated.
Server
Multiple virtual machines run on one physical server
Storage
Virtual storage is created from shared physical disks
Network
Virtual networks are created over shared physical network hardware
Desktop
Virtual desktops can be accessed remotely from different devices
Application
Applications can run in isolated virtual environments
Hypervisor
the software layer that creates and manages VMs
Physical server
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "physical server block at bottom, hypervisor layer above it, five branches on top labelled Server, Storage, Network, Desktop, Application, each leading to a virtual icon." The five TR bullets are the five branch cards, so each string appears once. The TR's closing line ("A hypervisor, the software layer that creates and manages VMs, sits between the physical hardware and each virtual resource") is the middle layer: the figure shows "sits between". TR speaker notes: "Emphasise that virtualization applies one abstraction principle to five different resource categories, not just computation. Interviewers often ask for all five types in order, so list server, storage, network, desktop and application together."
slides.label: Virtualization landscape

slides.title: Mechanism And Effect
slides.body:
Three Core Benefits
Before virtualization, each physical server typically ran one operating system and one application, leaving most capacity idle.
1fr 300px
Benefit
How Achieved
Effect
Consolidation
Multiple VMs share one physical host
Fewer physical servers needed for same workload
Isolation
Hypervisor enforces separate memory and CPU for each VM
A fault in one VM cannot affect others
Utilization
Idle CPU/memory cycles reassigned across VMs on demand
Average server utilization rises sharply versus one-app-per-server
Server utilization
Before
one app per server
Low
After
many VMs per server
High
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Small bar icon beside the table contrasting low utilization before virtualization with high utilization after." The TR gives no numbers, so the bars are schematic and say Low and High rather than a percentage. TR speaker notes: "Note that hypervisor-enforced isolation is what stops a crashed or compromised VM from affecting others sharing the host. Interviewers frequently ask why virtualization raises utilization: tie the answer to dynamic reallocation of idle cycles."
slides.label: Three core benefits

slides.title: Full OS For Each VM
slides.body:
Server Virtualization
Server virtualization means running multiple virtual servers on a single physical server, so its CPU, memory, and storage are shared instead of sitting idle. Each virtual server is called a virtual machine (VM) and works like an independent computer.
Server Virtualization
SERVER
VM
APP
OS
Hypervisor
Storage
CPU
RAM
Network
Internet
User
Cloud Computing
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN (course rule 3): one SERVER holding four VMs, each with three apps on its own OS, on one hypervisor, on the server's storage, CPU, RAM and network; the server reaches users over the internet, which is cloud computing. Same boxes, same places, same names as the source, filed in the central asset library under illustrations, cloud_computing, 3_virtualization_and_hypervisors.
slides.label: Server virtualization

slides.title: Pooled Virtual Volumes
slides.body:
Storage Virtualization
Storage virtualization pools capacity from multiple physical disks into logical volumes, letting applications see storage independent of the hardware beneath.
1fr 470px
Applications do not need to know which disk holds their data
Volumes can be resized without moving data manually
Snapshots: point-in-time copies for quick recovery
Replication: copies kept in another location for safety
AWS example: Amazon EBS provides virtual disks for EC2
Disk 1
Disk 2
Disk 3
Disk 4
Virtual Volume
Application
Amazon EBS
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "several physical disk icons feeding into a single pooled cylinder labelled Virtual Volume, with an application drawing from the cylinder." TR speaker notes: "Storage virtualization lets a volume resize or migrate without touching the physical array. Contrast with RAID, which protects fixed disks rather than pooling them."
slides.label: Storage virtualization

slides.title: A Bank's Shared Pool
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A bank combines money from multiple branches into a shared pool that customers can access from anywhere. Similarly, storage virtualization combines capacity from multiple physical disks into a single logical storage pool that applications can use without needing to know where the data is physically stored." The markers light 1, 2, 3 on both sides together: branches are disks, the pool is the virtual volume, the customer at any ATM is the application that never asks which branch.
slides.label: Analogy: a bank's shared pool

slides.title: Logical Nets Over Physical
slides.body:
Network Virtualization
Network virtualization uses software to create multiple separate virtual networks on top of one shared physical network. Each virtual network has its own addressing and settings.
PHYSICAL SERVER
VM
VM network
Hypervisor kernel
Physical network
Client
Storage array
pNIC
vNIC
pNIC: Physical NIC
vNIC: Virtual NIC
Network virtualization in a virtual data centre (VDC)
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN (course rule 3), with its caption "Network Virtualization In VDC" (VDC expanded, content rule 24): two physical servers, each with three VMs joined through virtual NICs to a VM network beside the hypervisor kernel; each server leaves through its physical NIC to one physical network, which also reaches a client and a storage array. NIC is the network interface card. Point at the two layers: the VM network inside each server is software, the physical network between them is cable.
slides.label: Network virtualization

slides.title: Logical Nets Over Physical
slides.body:
Network Virtualization
1fr 500px
Virtual switches replace physical wiring changes
Overlay networks tunnel traffic across shared links
Isolation prevents one tenant's traffic reaching another's
AWS example: Amazon VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) isolated network
One physical network cable
Amazon VPC
Network A
10.0.1.0/24
Network B
10.0.2.0/24
Network C
10.0.3.0/24
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "one physical network cable branching into several coloured logical network loops, each labelled with its own address range." The three ranges are example private address ranges, one per network, to make "its own addressing" visible; the TR names none. The padlocks between loops are the isolation bullet. TR speaker notes: "Network virtualization is the basis of software-defined networking (SDN), separating logical topology from physical cabling. A VPC is a fully isolated virtual network, unlike a VLAN which only segments one physical LAN."
slides.label: Network virtualization: logical networks

slides.title: A Wi-Fi For Each Company
slides.notes: SHARPENED FROM THE TR, which reads, verbatim: "A building can use one shared electricity connection while separate meters track each tenant's usage. Similarly, network virtualization uses one physical network to create multiple separate logical networks, each with its own addressing and access rules." Meters show separate measurement but not separate addressing or access, which is what the slide is about. One building, one cable in, and a Wi-Fi network for each company with its own name and its own password, maps all three: the cable is the physical network, each Wi-Fi is a virtual network with its own addressing, the password is the access rule. Say the TR sentence too if the room prefers it.
slides.label: Analogy: a Wi-Fi for each company

slides.title: Remote Access Delivery
slides.body:
Desktop & App Virtualization
Desktop virtualization delivers a full desktop from a remote host; application virtualization streams or isolates without local installation.
1fr 520px
Desktop: full OS session streamed remotely
Application: only the app runs remotely
Both remove dependency on local hardware
AWS examples: Amazon WorkSpaces desktops, AppStream 2.0 apps
Remote data centre
Full Desktop
Single App
Amazon WorkSpaces
AppStream 2.0
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "a remote data-centre icon streaming two outputs to a local screen: one labelled Full Desktop, one labelled Single App." The AppStream 2.0 mark is not in the current AWS architecture icon package, so that line carries the AWS mark. TR speaker notes: "Desktop virtualization, or virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI), delivers a whole session, while application virtualization streams just one app, a common interview mix-up. Both remove local installation and local hardware dependence."
slides.label: Desktop and app virtualization

slides.title: A Channel Or One Show
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Cable TV delivers a channel without a studio at home, just as desktop and app virtualization deliver a desktop or an app from a remote host without local installation." Kept, and split in two so it maps the difference the slide is about: the whole channel on the TV is the full desktop, one show on a tablet is the single app. The studio is never in the house.
slides.label: Analogy: cable TV

slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Full-width table as the sole visual; no additional diagram needed on this slide." The TR's last cell starts lower case ("remotely streamed or isolated app"); capitalised to match its column. TR speaker notes: "This table maps each type to its resource and a real AWS example, useful for fast recall. Only server virtualization runs a full guest OS; the other four abstract a resource without running one."
